# Carbon capture and storage is at a pivotal moment for decarbonization. Here's why

![Carbon capture and storage will grow to capture 6% of global CO2 emissions in 2050, up from just 0.5% in 2030.](https://assets.weforum.org/article/image/large_X3Iy_wMkpCkS4nQhoD7M9iMl9mZPFZijXLp5fbOVtSg.JPG)

Carbon capture and storage will grow to capture 6% of global CO2 emissions in 2050, up from just 0.5% in 2030. Image: Reuters

##### [Sverre Alvik](https://www.weforum.org/stories/authors/sverre-alvik/)

Carbon capture and storage (CCS) is critical to the energy transition. It is often the most feasible decarbonization technology for process industries such as cement, steel and chemical production. Yet, it has failed to scale, until now.

DNV’s [recently-released *Energy Transition Outlook: CCS to 2050*](https://www.dnv.com/energy-transition-outlook/carbon-capture-storage/) report shows that carbon capture and storage – which captures carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions at source, before being released into the atmosphere – is at a turning point. We expect it to grow fourfold to 2030 and this is backed up by developments in the CCS industry.

[Northern Lights](https://norlights.com/news/green-light-for-co2-injection-and-storage/), the world’s first open-source CO2 transport and storage infrastructure, in Western Norway, received its first shipment of liquified carbon dioxide from Heidelberg Materials in May. Meanwhile, [1PointFive’s STRATOS](https://www.1pointfive.com/carbon-removal) facility in Texas is about to come into operation and it will be the world’s [largest direct air capture (DAC) facility](https://www.1pointfive.com/news/1pointfive-holds-groundbreaking).

Here we demonstrate why DNV regards this as a pivotal moment for CCS.

## Why the turning point on carbon capture and storage is now

Cumulative investments in CCS in the coming five years are expected to [reach about $80billion](https://www.dnv.com/news/2025/turning-point-for-ccs-is-now-dnv-report-finds-with-global-capture-and-storage-capacity-expected-to-quadruple-by-2030/). Approximately two-thirds of the projected capacity additions will occur in North America and Europe, with North America also being the present leader.

We expect policy-driven growth in CCS capacity to lower costs by about 14% by 2030, mainly due to reductions in capital costs for capture technologies and in transport and storage costs.

![Carbon capture and storage capacity additions to 2030.](https://assets.weforum.org/editor/GK2NVusBupDNR93TiiMrVYw8kp3LKpisHUnCsHO-i9Y.png)

The hard-to-decarbonize sectors are where CCS has the most important role. Society will continue to need cement, fertilizer, steel and alike, which are produced through high energy processes that cannot be simply electrified.

The initial heavy lifting of CCS is being done by companies with their roots in the oil and gas sector. Northern Lights is a joint venture between Equinor, Shell and TotalEnergies while STRATOS is partly owned by Occidental, which is a reflection of the scale and complexity of the engineering involved as well as the investment required.

Most of the CCS deployment from known projects will be driven by decarbonizing the hydrocarbon production sectors (natural gas processing and low-carbon hydrogen and ammonia), where capturing carbon is generally cheaper due to higher CO2 concentrations and existing infrastructure.

After 2030, the strongest growth will be in hard-to-decarbonize sectors, with manufacturing accounting for 41% of annual CO2 captured by mid-century.

Manufacturing, particularly cement and chemicals, will be the biggest application of CCS in Europe; in North America and the Middle East, it will be hydrogen and ammonia; in China, coal power.

![Carbon capture and storage in 2030 and 2050.](https://assets.weforum.org/editor/AExv3GIn2RVyBfTbxAAqCMMb2orZl0Vdud-F_083h-k.png)

CCS will grow to capture 6% of global CO2 emissions in 2050 compared to just 0.5% in 2030, according to our estimates.

However, although this is impressive growth, it would have to grow six times more than forecast to achieve the volume needed for CCS in DNV’s [Pathway to Net Zero Emissions by 2050](https://www.dnv.com/publications/pathway-to-net-zero-emissions-report-2023-249543/) scenario.

![Share of global CO2 emissions captured with carbon capture and storage.](https://assets.weforum.org/editor/hPln3sEQWhJy5tzqtluDijVn7Q9pnGoEWOAxfN220yk.png)

It is much cheaper to reduce emissions now than to try and retrieve them in the future. However, we are a long way from achieving net zero emissions by 2050 and we will need carbon dioxide removal technologies, such as [direct air capture](https://www.weforum.org/stories/2023/04/explainer-what-is-direct-air-capture-and-how-can-it-fight-climate-change-1fe32b2dbb/) – that extracts CO2 from the atmosphere at any location – to play an important role in reducing the carbon overshoot for the decades to come.

These technologies are expensive, but the carbon market will be supportive to growth. By 2050, about one-quarter of captured emissions will be captured through carbon dioxide removal.

## **Leadership key to carbon capture and storage growth**

The growth of CCS is dependent on government leadership. The [Acorn Project](https://theacornproject.uk/) in Scotland recently secured government backing, however the opposition to the project demonstrates why advocates of CCS must navigate complicated political waters.

In the case of Acorn, there remains scepticism from the Green Party, who see CCS as a way of [extending the influence of the oil and gas industry](https://greenparty.org.uk/2024/10/07/green-party-reaction-to-fossil-fuel-lobbying-for-carbon-capture-and-storage/), and right-wing Reform UK, who [do not see net zero ambitions as a priority](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62k75qp1edo).

Security has become the defining feature of energy policy around the globe. As the growth of CCS is reliant on government support, the shifting policy priorities provides a significant downside risk to CCS. There are though encouraging signs from the public sector, where we have seen major projects given the green light, and the business world.

The likes of ExxonMobil, Shell, BP, Chevron, and Aramco have announced individual CCS targets ranging from 10 to 30 MtCO2/yr by 2030. Major investments and acquisitions related to CCS are becoming more frequent and substantial.

In 2023, ExxonMobil acquired Denbury for $4.9bn, gaining access to its CO2 pipeline infrastructure. SLB acquired a majority stake in Aker Carbon Capture, while Occidental purchased Carbon Engineering for $1.1bn, followed more recently by its acquisition of a second DAC company, Holocene.

The political journey for CCS is maybe as complicated as the technological solution. But if we are to maintain a focus on ultimately reaching net zero emissions and continue to benefit from the goods produced by heavy industry then the world will need CCS. Now is the turning point for CCS and we should work together to accelerate it further.

# Carbon Capture and Storage

An unproven technology that cannot meet planetary CO2 mitigation needs

Carbon capture and storage (CCS) is an expensive and unproven technology that distracts from global decarbonization efforts while allowing the oil and gas industry to conduct business as usual.

Even if realized at its full announced potential, CCS will only account for about [2.4% of the world’s carbon mitigation](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/sixth-assessment-report-cycle/) by 2030, according to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). It’s worth noting that not one single CCS project has ever reached its target CO2 capture rate.

[![ccs cop28 v2](/sites/default/files/inline-images/CCS_COP28_factsheet_v2.png)](https://ieefa.org/resources/fact-sheet-carbon-capture-and-storage)

*¹ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. [AR6 Synthesis Report](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/sixth-assessment-report-cycle/), Section 4.5 and Figure 4.4. March 2023.*

If its efficacy is questionable, its financial rationale is worse. Projects from [Algeria](https://ieefa.org/resources/carbon-capture-has-long-history-failure) to [Texas](https://ieefa.org/resources/ill-fated-petra-nova-ccs-project-nrg-energy-throws-towel) demonstrate the technology’s troubled history of cost overruns and delays. Yet an IEEFA review of 16 projects finds that even though the industry claims a 95% capture rate is achievable, no existing project has consistently captured more than 80% of carbon.

![ieefa real world carbon rate](/sites/default/files/inline-images/2023-12-05%20IEEFA%20Real%20world%20carbon%20capture%20rates.jpg)

*Last updated December 5, 2023. Originally appeared in IEEFA report *[Blue Hydrogen: Not clean, not low carbon, not a solution](https://ieefa.org/resources/blue-hydrogen-not-clean-not-low-carbon-not-solution).**

For the hundreds of currently proposed CO2 disposal projects, there is scant information on the technical efficacy of their underground storage sites. An [IEEFA study](https://ieefa.org/resources/norways-sleipner-and-snohvit-ccs-industry-models-or-cautionary-tales) explored the unexpected challenges faced and interventions needed in two Norwegian projects touted as successes, offering cautionary tales for proposals that are at least 10 times larger.

According to both the IPCC and International Energy Agency, we already hold the key to most CO2 mitigation: Renewable energy, energy efficiency, and eliminating fugitive methane emissions can address more than 80% of the world’s decarbonization requirements by 2030. CCS, even if its technical deficiencies can be overcome, can only provide minimal contribution to decarbonization. CCS does not deserve the equal billing that fossil fuel preservationists are giving it next to proven solutions.

For more, read our [reports and analysis](https://ieefa.org/topic/carbon-capture-and-storage) on CCS worldwide.

### “Proponents of [CCS] projects are selling an unproven dream that in all likelihood will become a nightmare for unsuspecting investors.”

Dennis Wamsted, Energy Analyst, IEEFA

[Read the Report](https://ieefa.org/articles/ieefa-us-mothballing-petra-nova-carbon-capture-project-shows-likely-fate-other-coal-fired)

### “Subsurface CO2 storage is an amalgamation of probabilities and risks ... these risks – and the costs that accompany them – are not being made part of public discourse by either industry or government."

Grant Hauber, Strategic Energy Finance Advisor, Asia, IEEFA

[Read the Report](https://ieefa.org/resources/norways-sleipner-and-snohvit-ccs-industry-models-or-cautionary-tales)

### “Given the amount of funds involved and the exposure of taxpayer dollars to risk, the U.S. government must implement robust due diligence and get beyond the advertising hype to the actual facts about carbon capture technology.”

Suzanne Mattei, Energy Policy Analyst, IEEFA, and David Schlissel, Director of Resource Planning Analysis, IEEFA

[Read the Report](https://ieefa.org/resources/ill-fated-petra-nova-ccs-project-nrg-energy-throws-towel)

### "CCS is just not competitive with renewable-based solutions - neither on cost nor on emissions. The capital cost of coal generation with CCS is expected to be about six times higher than large solar plants in 2030."

Amandine Denis-Ryan, CEO IEEFA Australia

Carbon capture (*i.e.*, CO2 capture) and storage (CCS) and carbon capture and utilization (CCU) are recognized as potential pathways to combat global climate change. Numerous efforts are underway, such as CCS (*e.g.*, biochar used for soil amendment; captured carbon injected into onshore or offshore reservoirs) and CCU (captured CO2 used for crop/algae production), due to enormous societal, economic and environmental concerns on climate change and for complying with emission regulations as well as meeting the committed emission reduction targets. This study compiled information on greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reduction initiatives, including CCS and CCU on the earth, recent technological advances in CCS and CCU, and their economic, environmental and societal implications. The prospect of CCS and CCU technologies has also been discussed. CCS processes require less energy compared with CCU and thus tend to be more cost-effective than CCU. The global warming potential (GWP) and the cost of energy systems that deployed CCS/CCU varied from 0.007–0.225 kg CO2 eq per MJ and $0.017–0.070 MJ−1, respectively. Both CCS and CCU have challenges, and public perception of these initiatives seems to be complex or not satisfactory for deploying large-scale projects, which hinders meeting the GHG emission reduction targets of different jurisdictions. The acceptance of CCU seems to be higher compared to that of CCS because of the concerns about land-use complexities. For a carbon-neutral economy, a single transition pathway appears to be inadequate. Stringent policies, financial incentives/benefits, stakeholder participation and technological advances would be crucial for the transition; however, technological advances and policy initiatives must be justified by a broader sustainability check to avoid the risk of investment and climate change.

# The Environmental Impacts of Carbon Capture and Storage

[Carbon Capture Technologies](https://blog.verde.ag/en/category/carbon-capture-technologies/)

As the world continues to grapple with the effects of climate change, it has become increasingly important to explore and develop technologies that can help reduce carbon emissions. One such technology is carbon capture and storage (CCS), which involves capturing carbon dioxide emissions from point sources such as industrial plants and power stations and storing them underground. While CCS has the potential to significantly reduce carbon emissions, there are concerns surrounding its environmental impacts. Read more about this topic.

## Some concerns about Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS)

[Carbon capture and storage (CCS) technology](https://blog.verde.ag/en/carbon-capture-introduction/) is increasingly being viewed as a potential solution to combat climate change. It offers a way to reduce the amount of carbon dioxide (CO2) emitted into the atmosphere while still allowing the continued use of fossil fuels. However, like any technology, CCS has its drawbacks.

One of the main concerns about CCS is the potential for carbon dioxide to leak from its storage sites over time. The term leakage, or seepage, in this context is referred to undesired CO2 losses to the atmosphere due to infrastructure or storage malfunctions.

While there is currently no commercial-scale CCS operation, leakage has been observed in some pilot and demonstration projects. The risks associated with leakage include the potential for harm to ecosystems and human health.

However, it should be noted that many experts consider the risks associated with CCS to be relatively low compared to those associated with continuing to emit carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

Another concern regarding CCS is the amount of water used in the capture process. CCS requires large volumes of water to facilitate the capture of carbon dioxide from industrial processes.

While the amount of water used in CCS is generally lower than that used in conventional power plants, concerns have been raised regarding potential impacts on local water resources.

Despite these concerns, many proposed CCS projects have taken steps to address water use issues, such as using non-potable water sources or implementing closed-loop systems that recirculate water.

There are also potential environmental impacts of Carbon Capture and Storage.

## Potential environmental impacts of Carbon Capture and Storage

CCS can also have land use impacts, particularly in areas where pipelines or storage sites are located. The land use impacts of CCS will depend on various factors, including the size of the project and the sensitivity of the local environment.

Where possible, CCS projects should be designed to minimize land use impacts. In some cases, the setting up of Carbon Capture and Storage facilities may also lead to conflicts with local communities, highlighting the importance of ensuring that CCS projects are transparent and engage with local stakeholders.

One possible solution to these challenges concerning environmental impacts of CCS is the use of technologies that poses less impacts, such as [Enhanced Rock Weathering (ERW)](https://blog.verde.ag/en/enhanced-rock-weathering-intro/), which can capture carbon from the atmosphere and store it in the soil via a natural process and which implementation generates less disturbances on the overall environment.

Also, it is worth noting that Carbon Capture and Storage is not a silver bullet solution to the problem of climate change. Rather, it should be seen as one tool in a broader suite of technologies and policy measures to reduce carbon emissions.

For example, CCS could be paired with renewable energy technologies such as wind and solar power to create a more balanced, low-carbon energy system.

Moreover, CCS should not be used as an excuse to maintain the status quo in high-emitting sectors such as the fossil fuel industry. Rather, efforts should be made to accelerate the transition to cleaner and more sustainable forms of energy production.

## CCS is an important tool to mitigate climate changes, and its risks are relatively low

Summarizing, carbon capture and storage has the potential to significantly reduce carbon emissions from industry and power generation. However, it is important to carefully consider the environmental impacts of this technology, including potential leakage, water use, and land use changes.

While there are risks associated with Carbon Capture and Storage, many experts consider them to be relatively low compared to the risks associated with continuing to emit [carbon dioxide into the atmosphere](https://blog.verde.ag/pt/encontro-com-gigantes/como-o-manejo-agricola-pode-ajudar-a-reduzir-emissoes-de-gases-de-efeito-estufa/). Also, [there is a variety of technologies that can be more beneficial with less impact, such as ERW](https://blog.verde.ag/en/carbon-capture-climate-solutions/).

Moreover, it is important to bear in mind that CCS should be seen as one tool in a broader suite of technologies and policy measures to reduce carbon emissions. By taking a balanced and integrated approach to tackling climate change, we can create a more sustainable and prosperous future for all.

## Carbon Capture and Storage

## What is carbon capture and storage?

Carbon capture and storage (CCS) and carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) are processes designed to collect or “capture” carbon dioxide generated by high-emitting activities like coal- or gas-fired power production or plastics manufacturing. Those captured emissions are then transported to sites where they are used for industrial processes or stored underground.

CCS does not remove carbon from the atmosphere. At best, CCS prevents some emissions caused by the combustion of carbon-based fuels from reaching the atmosphere — provided that the captured gases are not later released.

In practice, CCS:

## Open letter to policymakers

On July 19th, 2021, over 500 international, US, and Canadian organizations sent an open letter to policymakers calling on them to “reject carbon capture and storage.” The letter was accompanied by ads in The Washington Post and The Hill Times.

Read the full open letters to [US](https://www.ciel.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/CCS-Letter_FINAL_US-1.pdf) and [Canadian](https://www.ciel.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/CCS-Letter_FINAL_CAN-1.pdf) policymakers.

Read [statements from organizational leaders](https://www.ciel.org/organizations-demand-policymakers-reject-carbon-capture-and-storage/) on the dangers of carbon capture.

See the ads in [The Washington Post](https://www.ciel.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/CCS-Ad_The-Washington-Post_FINAL.pdf) and Ottawa’s [The Hill Times](https://www.ciel.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/CCS-Ad_The-Hill-Times_FINAL.pdf).

## Seven reasons why policymakers should reject carbon capture and storage

### 1. The buildout of CCS infrastructure presents serious health, safety, and environmental risks. Marginalized communities already overburdened by industrial hazards are being targeted for CCS.

Transporting and storing carbon dioxide (CO2) involves a massive network of perilous pipelines connected to underground injection sites, each with its own set of dangers. Pipelines can leak or rupture; compressed CO2 is highly hazardous upon release and can result in the asphyxiation of humans and animals. Underground storage poses additional risks, such as potential leakage, contamination of drinking water, and stimulation of seismic activity. These hazards apply to all the current and proposed variants utilizing CCS technologies, including carbon capture utilization and storage (CCUS), fossil hydrogen with CCS (“blue” or decarbonized hydrogen), bioenergy with CCS (BECCS), coal-bioenergy systems with CCS (CBECCS), waste-to-energy with CCS (WtE-CCS), and direct air capture (DAC), which depends on CCS or CCUS to manage the captured carbon.

### 2. CCS is not consistent with the principles of environmental justice.

Pollution-burdened communities are being targeted for CCS, which brings new risks and threats, ironically in the name of environmental justice. The U.S. Gulf Coast, including the Louisiana petrochemical corridor known as “Cancer Alley,” northern plains, and California Central Valley, and the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan in Canada, are among those areas being targeted for CCS development. Such a buildout would impose new pollution and safety hazards on Black, Brown, and Indigenous communities already suffering the disproportionate and deadly impacts of environmental racism.

### 3. Rather than replacing fossil fuels, carbon capture technology prolongs our dependence on them.

By design, carbon capture is parasitic on the underlying sources of emissions to which it is attached. Putting carbon capture technology on greenhouse-gas emitting facilities enables those facilities to continue operating, effectively providing those emitters with a license to pollute indefinitely. In practice, CCS at best captures only a fraction of carbon emissions and fails to address other harmful pollution from fuel combustion, such as fine particulate matter (PM2.5), as well as other contaminants from the underlying activities to which CCS was applied. The additional energy required to power the carbon capture process generates even more emissions if supplied by fossil fuels.

### 4. The majority of captured carbon is used to pump more oil out of the ground.

Almost all existing CCS projects are tied to “enhanced oil recovery” (EOR). In EOR, CO2 is injected into depleted underground oil reservoirs to boost oil production. EOR is currently the primary market driver for captured CO2; no other markets exist at the scale proposed by many of the technology’s proponents. EOR results in more oil extraction and more carbon emissions when that oil is burned and is disastrous for the climate. Yet, the public in the United States is currently paying for EOR through the Section 45Q tax credit, of which oil companies are the biggest beneficiaries. In Canada, the oil and gas industry is lobbying for a similar tax break.

### 5. There is no economic rationale for the massive deployment of CCS.

Attaching carbon capture technology to an emitting source makes operating that source both more expensive and more energy-intensive. As costs of clean energy like solar and wind plummet, fossil fuel and biomass power plants are becoming less competitive, and adding carbon capture just makes them more costly. Even in heavy-emitting industrial sectors such as plastic or petrochemical manufacturing, applying CCS at scale makes little climate or economic sense.

The push to deploy CCS in the industrial sector ignores the most important alternative methods for curtailing the vast majority of the sector’s emissions. These methods, including replacing fossil fuels with non-carbon emitting renewable energy, are already available and scalable. Investing in CCS infrastructure add-ons to existing facilities locks those facilities and their current energy technologies in place. It diverts resources from non-polluting alternatives that are compatible with a safe climate future.

### 6. CCS does not remove CO2 from the atmosphere. At best, it prevents some carbon emissions from entering the atmosphere.

Even there, it falls short: CCS projects implemented to date have systematically overpromised and under-delivered on emissions reductions. Advertisements from some fossil fuel companies that compare CCS to a living plant are deeply misleading. Industry claims that BECCS is a negative emissions technology are based on the flawed and scientifically discredited premise that burning biomass is carbon neutral. In fact, burning wood for energy can increase greenhouse gas impacts for decades to centuries compared to fossil fuels.

### 7. Science and existing regulations do not back the promise of “permanent” storage or sequestration of carbon.

Current US federal regulations, for example, only require storage of CO2 for 50 years to qualify for subsidies. But CO2 lingers in the atmosphere and environment on a geological time scale — for hundreds or even thousands of years. Considering CO2 injected underground or used in the manufacture of plastics, cement, or other goods will be safely contained in perpetuity is irresponsible at best. It merely kicks the can down a very short road, to be a burden to the next generation.

Carbon Capture, Utilisation, and Storage (CCUS) is an essential technology for reducing carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions and supporting the transition to a net-zero energy system. However, like any industrial process, CCUS carries certain risks that must be carefully addressed, in this case, particularly due to the large volumes of CO2 involved and operational conditions associated with carbon dioxide’s unique properties.

This blog provides an overview of the key safety concerns related to CO2 in CCUS technology, highlights examples of accidents involving large CO2 releases, and outlines the measures in place to protect both people and the environment.

## How CCUS works

CCUS involves capturing CO2 from industrial sources, transporting it, and either storing it or using it in other applications. Let’s take a look at how the process works in a nutshell.

![Carbon Capture, Utilisation, and Storage (CCUS) process](data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB3aWR0aD0iMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIxIiB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciPjwvc3ZnPg==)

**Figure 1**. CCUS process (Source: Shutterstock)

### Capture

The first step in CCUS is capturing CO2 emissions from large-scale industrial processes, such as power generation, cement production, or chemical manufacturing. There are several methods to capture CO2:

* Pre-combustion capture1:  Pre-combustion capture involves removing CO2 from fuels prior to combustion. The process begins with the gasification of the fuel to produce syngas—a mixture of hydrogen, carbon monoxide, CO2, and other gases. The syngas is then subjected to a water-gas shift reaction, converting CO and water into hydrogen and CO2. Finally, the CO2 is separated, leaving behind a hydrogen-rich fuel ready for combustion.

* Post-combustion capture2: This method captures CO2 from flue gases after combustion. It’s the most commonly used method in power plants and can be retrofitted to existing facilities.

* Oxy-fuel combustion3: Fuel is burned in pure oxygen instead of air, producing a flue gas that is mainly CO2, making the separation process more efficient.

Once captured, the CO2 is compressed into a liquefied state for easier transportation.

### Transportation

After capture, CO2 is transported to either a storage location or a utilisation site. This is usually done through pipelines, but trucks, ships, and even trains can be used for smaller quantities or when pipelines are not feasible. Pipelines are the most common mode of transport, especially in regions with a well-established network for oil and gas.

### Utilisation

Captured CO2 can then be utilised in various applications, such as Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR), where it is injected into oil fields to boost extraction rates or in the production of chemicals, plastics, and even carbonated beverages. These uses not only add value but also help offset the costs associated with capturing and storing CO2.

### Storage

The final step involves permanently storing CO2 in geological formations, such as depleted oil and gas fields or deep saline aquifers. This process, known as geological sequestration, ensures that the CO2 is trapped securely and monitored over time to prevent leakage. Storage sites are carefully selected based on their ability to retain CO2 over long periods without risk of release.

## Key safety concerns in CCUS technology

While CCUS offers considerable environmental benefits, it also comes with safety challenges that must be managed for successful implementation. These challenges arise from the inherent risks associated with handling CO2, as well as the specific hazards present at each stage of the CCUS process.

Before discussing the risks of handling CO2, it’s important to understand its basic properties.

### Understanding CO2 properties

CO2 is a colourless, odourless gas that can be naturally present in the Earth’s atmosphere. It makes up about 0.04% of the air we breathe and is a byproduct of processes like respiration and combustion.

* Physical state

CO2 can exist in four states: gas, liquid, supercritical, and solid. Under normal atmospheric pressure, CO2 remains a gas, but when subjected to high pressure, it can be compressed into a liquid or, at very low temperatures, can be present as a solid (dry ice).

![CO2 can exist in four states: gas, liquid, supercritical, and solid. Under normal atmospheric pressure, CO2 remains a gas, but when subjected to high pressure, it can be compressed into a liquid or, at very low temperatures, can be present as a solid (dry ice). 

](data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB3aWR0aD0iMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIxIiB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciPjwvc3ZnPg==)

**Figure 2**. CO2 physical states.

* Weight and density

CO2 is 1.5 times heavier than air, so in the event of a leak, it behaves as a heavy gas, spreading close to the ground. This can result in accumulation in low-lying areas or confined spaces.

![COSHER joint industry project: Large-scale pipeline rupture tests to study CO2 release and dispersion](data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB3aWR0aD0iMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIxIiB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciPjwvc3ZnPg==)

**Figure 3**. COSHER joint industry project: Large-scale pipeline rupture tests to study CO2 release and dispersion.4

* Solubility

CO2 is highly soluble in water, forming carbonic acid (H₂CO₃). Prolonged exposure to carbonic acid in industrial environments can cause corrosion of equipment, leading to leaks and structural damage. To mitigate these risks, strict guidelines on CO2 impurities, especially on water content, are essential.

* Non-flammable but dangerous

CO2 is non-flammable, making it valuable for use in fire extinguishers. However, its non-toxic classification is misleading when dealing with high concentrations. When inhaled in large quantities, CO2 can cause dizziness, unconsciousness, and in extreme cases, death, due to a decrease in the amount of oxygen available for respiration.

![CO2 is non-flammable, making it valuable for use in fire extinguishers. However, its non-toxic classification is misleading when dealing with high concentrations. When inhaled in large quantities, CO2 can cause dizziness, unconsciousness, and in extreme cases, death, due to a decrease in the amount of oxygen available for respiration.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB3aWR0aD0iMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIxIiB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciPjwvc3ZnPg==)

Figure 4. Health effects of carbon dioxide exposure.

### CO2 hazards in CCUS technology

Although CO2 can be naturally present in the atmosphere and is generally considered harmless in small amounts, managing it in the large volumes required for CCUS presents significant risks.

* Dangerous at high concentrations

Exposure to CO2 levels above 0,5% (vol) (OSHA PEL (Permissible Exposure Limit) – TLV (Threshold Limit Value) for prolonged periods can cause symptoms such as headaches, dizziness, or nausea. At even higher concentrations, CO2 can lead to asphyxiation, with exposure to concentrations around 4% (vol) considered immediately dangerous to life and health (IDLH). ## Highlights

*   •Provides a comprehensive review of CCS technologies, from capture to storage, across key sectors, and maps the evolution of global CCS deployment. 
*   •Demonstrates that CCS offers cost-effective mitigation in hard-to-abate applications and complements renewable energy and electrification efforts. 
*   •Identifies policy, regulatory and market actions needed to accelerate CCS deployment toward net-zero targets. 

## Abstract

This Review examines the role of carbon capture and storage (CCS) in achieving net-zero emissions by 2050, focusing on its scale-up and integration across energy systems and hard-to-abate industries. Its interdisciplinary approach provides a comprehensive review of the state-of-the-art in CCS research, evaluating its potential role in achieving net-zero emissions. It assesses not only technological advancements and characteristics but also the critical costs and energy requirements of various CCS technologies. Based on modelling insights from the International Energy Agency Net Zero Emissions pathway, it highlights the need to scale CCS deployment to 1 Gt CO₂ annually by 2030 to stay on track for climate goals. This review piece underscores the urgency of rapid CCS scale-up this decade, complementing other measures across energy and industry. Furthermore, it assesses the recent advancements in CO₂ capture, transport, and storage technologies, along with their techno-economic characteristics and results in energy system models. The study concludes by identifying key challenges and providing a strategy roadmap for decision-makers for accelerating CCS deployment.

## Abstract

Climate change is driven by large greenhouse gas emissions, which have raised an alarm in efforts to reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide levels with CCS, drawing attention to decarbonization efforts. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of current Carbon Dioxide (CO 2) capture methods, including absorption, adsorption, and membrane separation and emerging Direct Air Capture (DAC), while addressing their limitations in cost, efficiency, and scalability. A key focus is the emerging role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in accelerating CCS deployment. AI-driven techniques, particularly machine learning, are being applied to optimize capture processes, improve system performance, and facilitate the discovery of advanced materials. We synthesize evidence on supervised and unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning and generative models mapped to concrete CCS tasks: sorbent/solvent screening, soft sensing, emissions forecasting, digital-twin control, and storage integrity surveillance This review also highlights recent advancements at the intersection of AI and CCS, evaluates their potential for large-scale implementation, and discusses remaining technical and policy challenges. The findings underscore the strategic importance of integrating AI to enhance the effectiveness and scalability of CCS in support of global decarbonization goals.

## Abstract

Climate change mitigation requires the large-scale deployment of carbon capture and storage (CCS). Recent plans indicate an eight-fold increase in CCS capacity by 2030, yet the feasibility of CCS expansion is debated. Using historical growth of CCS and other policy-driven technologies, we show that if plans double between 2023 and 2025 and their failure rates decrease by half, CCS could reach 0.37 GtCO 2 yr−1 by 2030—lower than most 1.5 °C pathways but higher than most 2 °C pathways. Staying on-track to 2 °C would require that in 2030–2040 CCS accelerates at least as fast as wind power did in the 2000s, and that after 2040, it grows faster than nuclear power did in the 1970s to 1980s. Only 10% of mitigation pathways meet these feasibility constraints, and virtually all of them depict <600 GtCO 2 captured and stored by 2100. Relaxing the constraints by assuming no failures of CCS plans and growth as fast as flue-gas desulfurization would approximately double this amount.
